title: Mechanism-guided prevention of major post-viral syndromes

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a reliable way to identify why particular groups of patients develop persistent illness after a viral infection, then intervene early enough to prevent clinically meaningful long-term disability. Its defining advance would be connecting an actionable causal mechanism, a patient group and an effective preventive intervention. This capability has not been demonstrated by the supplied evidence.

Long COVID provides the evidence base in the supplied record. The reviewed guideline discusses potentially different pathways, including persistent viral presence, immune or inflammatory changes and sustained tissue injury. These are plausible mechanisms rather than established explanations for every patient. Mechanism-guided prevention would require determining which pathways actually contribute to illness in particular groups and whether changing those pathways prevents persistent disease.

The concept encompasses major post-viral syndromes as a research goal, but evidence from long COVID cannot establish mechanisms or preventive efficacy for other syndromes. A successful intervention could apply to one pathway or patient group without covering every manifestation of long COVID, and extension to additional viruses would require separate evidence.

significance.text: Reliable prevention of a substantial share of persistent disability after infection would change the long-term consequences of epidemics and endemic disease. The guideline describes impaired quality of life and functional capacity, increased sick leave and substantial burdens on individuals, families and society. Preventing those outcomes would directly reduce illness extending beyond the acute infection; the scale of that benefit would depend on efficacy, eligibility, safety and access.

A further potential benefit would be making prevention more selective and interpretable: patients could receive an intervention because evidence identifies a relevant pathway, while trials could test whether disrupting that pathway changes long-term outcomes. This is a conditional implication of the proposed capability, not an established clinical benefit. A mechanism-guided approach would still need to demonstrate practical value beyond existing preventive strategies.

Success in one syndrome could guide research on others by suggesting useful biomarkers, trial designs or biological targets. It would not prove that different post-viral syndromes share a cause, that one treatment works across viruses or that all persistent symptoms are preventable. The potentially revolutionary impact rests on substantial, durable prevention in demonstrated populations, rather than on an assumption of universal applicability.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is reliable identification of actionable causal mechanisms in defined patient groups, coupled to prevention of functionally significant long-term illness. The reviewed guideline supports phenotype-driven trials and biomarker-informed patient stratification. Its discussion of persistence, injury and inflammation supplies candidate pathways, but does not establish which pathway causes which outcome in each patient.

A concrete scientific barrier is distinguishing a causal driver from a biological change that accompanies illness or follows tissue damage. As a synthesis of the research goal, a useful biomarker would need to do more than correlate with symptoms: it should help identify a relevant patient group, predict a preventive response or demonstrate that the intended pathway was altered. Candidate mechanisms may overlap, so one abnormal measurement need not identify a single sufficient cause.

Clinical and engineering barriers include selecting an effective intervention window, measuring durable functional benefit consistently and making patient selection feasible in routine care. Trials must also determine whether benefits justify adverse effects and treatment burden in people who might otherwise recover without persistent illness. The guideline's call for standardized outcomes and targeted trial designs supports this direction; the specific implementation requirements are a synthesis of what the proposed capability would need.

current_state.text: According to the supplied validated review of the full main article, the July 2026 Clinical practice guideline for long COVID prevention and treatment conditionally suggested COVID-19 vaccination and acute-phase antiviral treatment to prevent long COVID. The supporting evidence was rated very low certainty for vaccination and low certainty for antivirals. These recommendations indicate potential preventive benefit under uncertainty; they do not establish reliable, mechanism-guided prevention.

The guideline also reported a preventive signal from one metformin randomized trial, while finding insufficient evidence for routine non-antiviral prevention. A signal from one trial is relevant evidence, but does not by itself establish a replicated preventive strategy or identify the causal pathway and patient groups responsible for benefit. The supplied review provides no numerical effect estimate to preserve or independently assess.

The evidence account here rests on the supplied review, which reports that verified, untruncated full-text XML contained the main article and references. Linked supplementary appendices were not supplied. The earlier account of publisher and mirror access failures is not verified by this record and does not justify treating the guideline's recommendations as available only through indexed text.

The guideline mainly addresses adults and explicitly excludes emerging variants and outcomes beyond its search cutoff. The supplied record contains no freshness search establishing the complete research state through November 1, 2026. It also does not establish prevention across all post-viral syndromes. These boundaries limit the conclusions that can be drawn; they are not evidence that preventive effects outside the record are absent.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: replicated randomized trials should show that a preventive intervention with an acceptable safety profile substantially reduces prespecified, functionally significant post-viral illness over long follow-up. Protocols should define the clinically meaningful effect, follow-up duration, functional outcomes and safety assessment before results are known. These are proposed criteria for evaluating the innovation, not established standards attributed to the guideline.
completion_criteria.label: Replicated randomized trials show prevention’s functional benefits and acceptable safety

completion_criteria.text: To establish the mechanism-guided component, convincing evidence should connect patient selection and pathway engagement to preventive benefit. A proposed demonstration would combine a reproducible method for identifying eligible patients, evidence that the intervention changes the intended pathway and clinical results consistent with that mechanism. An effective intervention alone could establish prevention without resolving why it works; a biomarker association alone would not establish prevention.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible patient selection and pathway engagement connect to preventive benefit

completion_criteria.text: Replication should examine independent populations and relevant practical settings, with clearly reported limits on age, infection history, viral context, timing and access to testing or treatment. Studies should establish whether benefits persist, which outcomes improve and whether adverse effects or implementation burdens constrain use. Studies across additional viruses and syndromes would be required to extend the claim. Finite trials can establish demonstrated breadth within studied conditions, not literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Replication across populations and practical settings establishes benefits and limits

related_concepts.text: INF-10, Prevention of multiple sclerosis by controlling Epstein–Barr virus, has the closest conceptual overlap: both seek to prevent a later illness by acting on an infection-related causal pathway. INF-10 concerns a specified virus–disease relationship, whereas INF-14 seeks mechanism-guided prevention across potentially heterogeneous post-viral syndromes. Success in either would not establish the other's causal model or preventive efficacy.

INF-07, Broad-spectrum treatment for unrelated viral infections, could provide candidate interventions if suppressing a relevant infection prevents later illness, but activity against acute viral disease would not establish prevention of persistent disability. INF-08, A pre-emptive vaccine against diverse pandemic coronaviruses, and INF-09, A rapid, end-to-end vaccine response to a newly identified pathogen, concern vaccine protection and response capability. They could contribute upstream to prevention, while INF-14 specifically requires durable post-viral outcomes and evidence connecting mechanisms to benefit. These relationships are conceptual comparisons based on the supplied roster.

INF-05, Near-patient diagnosis of the cause and treatability of most serious infections, overlaps with the need to select an appropriate intervention. Identifying an infectious cause or its treatability, however, does not necessarily identify the pathway responsible for later persistent illness. INF-14 may require additional biological and functional stratification after the acute infection.

The other vaccine and transmission concepts—INF-01, A broadly protective HIV vaccine; INF-03, A tuberculosis vaccine that interrupts transmission; INF-04, A reliable way to break malaria transmission through its vectors; and INF-13, A highly protective, durable and readily deliverable malaria vaccine—share the broad aim of preventing disease burden. Their specified endpoints concern particular infections or transmission, whereas INF-14 concerns persistent illness following viral infection. Shared preventive intent does not make these interchangeable capabilities.

INF-02, A safe, scalable cure for established HIV infection, and INF-11, A safe, broadly effective treatment-free cure for chronic hepatitis B, concern established chronic viral infections. INF-14 includes persistent viral presence as one possible mechanism in long COVID, but does not assume that every post-viral syndrome is an ongoing infection requiring a virological cure. INF-12, Very short, reliable curative treatment for active and latent tuberculosis, INF-06, A dependable platform for generating new antibacterial treatments, and INF-15, A rapidly adaptable clinical phage-therapy platform, address distinct bacterial treatment capabilities. Their development and trial methods may offer general lessons, but their biological targets and completion endpoints remain separate.

unresolved_issues: Which candidate pathways are causal and actionable in which long-COVID patient groups remains unresolved in the supplied record.
The supplied review does not provide numerical preventive effect estimates, detailed metformin trial characteristics or the linked supplementary appendices.
The complete state of research through November 1, 2026, is not established because the supplied freshness search record is empty.
Preventive efficacy and mechanistic transfer to other post-viral syndromes require separate evidence.
Clinically meaningful effect sizes, follow-up duration, acceptable safety and feasible patient-selection methods remain to be operationally defined for the proposed demonstrations.
The earlier publisher and mirror access-failure claims remain unverified; they were omitted from the scientific evidence characterization rather than resolved as historical events.

brief.title: Preventing lasting illness after viral infections
possible: After a viral infection, people could receive early treatment matched to the biological cause of their risk of lasting illness. Doctors could identify which patients would benefit and intervene before persistent symptoms become long-term disability.
why: Preventing lasting illness would help people keep working and carrying out daily activities. It would reduce the burden of prolonged illness on families and change the long-term consequences of infections.
Knowing what drives illness in a particular patient group would give doctors a reason to choose a treatment. Researchers could test whether changing that cause actually prevents disability.

sources.who: Multidisciplinary Working Group on Long COVID Practice Guidelines
sources.showed: The group reviewed prevention research and conditionally recommended vaccination and drugs that fight the virus during COVID-19. Evidence for these preventive benefits had very low or low certainty.
sources.cited_for: The guideline supports possible prevention benefits and identifies biological processes that need further study.
sources.not_established: It does not establish which biological causes to target in particular patients to reliably prevent lasting disability.

sources.who: Carolyn T Bramante and the COVID-OUT Study Team
sources.showed: A randomized trial found fewer long COVID diagnoses among participants given metformin during early COVID-19. Participants were adults with overweight or obesity.
sources.cited_for: The trial provides evidence that early treatment can reduce later long COVID diagnoses.
sources.not_established: It does not establish replicated prevention of lasting functional disability or identify the biological cause of the benefit.

shown: The COVID-OUT team found a preventive benefit from metformin in a randomized trial, which assigns treatment by chance. This is a step toward prevention, but connecting a treatment's benefit to a specific biological cause in a defined patient group remains unfinished.
missing: Reliable tests that identify a treatable cause of persistent illness in a defined patient group are still needed.
Repeated trials have yet to establish substantial, lasting prevention of disability with acceptable safety.
Patient selection and early treatment still need to work in routine care.
Extending prevention beyond long COVID requires separate evidence for other viruses and lasting illnesses.

milestones.label: Repeated trials establish lasting benefit and acceptable safety
milestones.explanation: Repeated randomized trials would have to show substantially less lasting disability, using outcomes and safety criteria set beforehand. This would establish dependable prevention.

milestones.label: Patient selection and biological changes explain preventive benefit
milestones.explanation: Studies would have to reliably identify eligible patients and link treatment's effect on the intended biological process to prevention. This would connect who benefits with why treatment works.

milestones.label: Benefits and limits hold across populations and practical settings
milestones.explanation: Independent studies would have to establish durable benefits and limits across populations and care settings, with separate studies for other viruses. This would establish where prevention works and where it does not.

uncertain: It remains unclear which patient groups develop illness because of lingering virus, altered immune responses or lasting tissue damage.
The best treatment window and the tests needed to select patients remain unresolved.
How much benefit, how long a follow-up and what level of treatment risk should count as success remain to be defined.

page.title: Mechanism-guided prevention of long COVID
page.definition: During acute SARS-CoV-2 infection, a biomarker would identify adults likely to benefit from a treatment directed at a particular biological pathway. Randomized trials would show that the treatment changes that pathway and that the marker predicts who gains greater protection against long COVID that limits daily activities.

goal.need: In 2023, an estimated 6.4% of noninstitutionalized US adults had current long COVID. Among them, 19.8% said symptoms reduced their daily activities a lot. Vaccination and some acute treatments may lower overall risk, but an average benefit cannot tell a patient which treatment to take. If a test during acute infection reliably identifies who benefits enough to justify the harms, early treatment could help those patients retain daily function and spare others unnecessary drug exposure.

completion.title: Independent randomized trials establish pathway-matched prevention of function-limiting long COVID.
completion.criterion: Two independent randomized trials measure the pathway biomarker before treatment and compare treatment with control across marker values. Each verifies pathway engagement, meets its prespecified efficacy criterion in the intended marker-defined group, and shows greater preventive benefit in that group by a prespecified treatment-by-marker interaction. The endpoint is adult WHO-defined post-COVID-19 condition with measured impairment of daily function. Benefit and harms meet protocol-defined clinical criteria.
completion.set_by: Atlas operational criterion; no external body was found to have published this combined test.
completion.basis: WHO defines adult post-COVID-19 condition after probable or confirmed infection, usually three months from onset, with symptoms lasting at least two months and no alternative diagnosis. FDA guidance distinguishes efficacy in a marker-defined group from evidence that a marker predicts differential benefit. The Atlas combines these elements with measured functional impairment, pathway engagement and independent replication.

milestones.title: An antiviral candidate reduces infectious SARS-CoV-2 output by 50% in cell culture.
milestones.criterion: Determine the concentration at which the candidate reduces infectious SARS-CoV-2 output by 50% relative to the vehicle control in cell culture. Measure cell viability separately to assess whether cell loss accounts for the reduction.
milestones.set_by: The pharmacological IC50 convention, implemented by Parthasarathy et al., section 2.6 and Figure 4. This laboratory test concerns the antiviral route.
milestones.threshold_quote: IC50 and IC90 were calculated from PFU data from metformin titration experiments.

milestones.title: Acute treatment lowers nasal SARS-CoV-2 RNA across days 5 and 10 in COVID-OUT.
milestones.criterion: In the randomized nasal-swab substudy, show lower overall follow-up viral RNA with active treatment than with matched placebo. Use the day 5 and day 10 nasal RNA measurements in log10 copies/mL, adjusting for day 1 viral RNA in the prespecified analysis.
milestones.set_by: COVID-OUT investigators, prespecified statistical analysis plan for NCT04510194, described in the peer-reviewed virologic report. This endpoint concerns antiviral activity.
milestones.threshold_quote: The virologic secondary end point was overall viral load in follow-up, adjusted for baseline viral load as prespecified in the SAP.

milestones.title: Acute treatment reduces clinician diagnoses of long COVID through day 300 at two-sided p<0.05.
milestones.criterion: In COVID-OUT, compare time from randomization to a participant-reported clinician diagnosis of long COVID between an active drug and its matched placebo. Ascertain diagnosis dates in surveys on days 180, 210, 240, 270 and 300. Require fewer diagnoses over follow-up by a two-sided log-rank test at p<0.05. Eligible outpatients were aged 30–85 years, had overweight or obesity, had symptoms for fewer than seven days and had tested positive within three days before enrolment.
milestones.set_by: COVID-OUT investigators, NCT04510194 long-term outcome and statistical analysis methods. The population and endpoint are specific to this protocol.
milestones.threshold_quote: with a two-sided p value of less than 0·05 as the criterion for statistical significance.

milestones.title: The probability that metformin lowers day-180 symptom or death risk reaches 0.975 in ACTIV-6.
milestones.criterion: Compare 14 days of metformin with placebo in adults treated during acute COVID-19. The event is death by day 180 or any participant-reported COVID-19 symptom on day 180, excluding symptoms after a new infection reported within the preceding 28 days. In the modified intention-to-treat analysis, the posterior probability that the adjusted absolute risk difference favors metformin must reach 0.975 under the rule adopted after the day-28 analysis.
milestones.set_by: ACTIV-6 investigators, master protocol NCT04885530 and metformin appendix NCT06042855. The day-180 report specifies the revised probability threshold.
milestones.threshold_quote: require a PPE of 0.975 for the risk difference of PASC on day 180.

milestones.title: A randomized trial meets its long COVID prevention endpoint in prespecified marker-positive adults.
milestones.criterion: Define the pathway marker and the marker-positive population before treatment. Within that population, compare early treatment with a randomized control and demonstrate a reduction in the prespecified clinical long COVID endpoint under the trial’s type I error control plan.
milestones.set_by: US FDA, Enrichment Strategies guidance, section VI.B.2. This general predictive-enrichment criterion is applied to prevention here; FDA supplies no long-COVID-specific effect size.
milestones.threshold_quote: a statistically rigorous demonstration of the treatment effect in the marker-positive patients

milestones.title: A pretreatment biomarker assay meets validation criteria for its intended use.
milestones.criterion: For a pathway marker measured as a concentration in a clinical specimen, validate the assay in the intended specimen type and across the concentration range used for selection. Document its accuracy, precision, sensitivity, selectivity, reproducibility and stability, and justify the acceptance criteria for that use.
milestones.set_by: US FDA, Bioanalytical Method Validation for Biomarkers, section III, applied to a concentration assay used for patient selection.
milestones.threshold_quote: a fit-for-purpose approach should be used when determining the appropriate extent of method validation.

milestones.title: Nirmatrelvir–ritonavir reduces the three-month symptom endpoint at two-sided p<0.05.
milestones.criterion: In PANORAMIC Norway, compare five days of nirmatrelvir–ritonavir with placebo in nonhospitalized adults aged 18–65 years with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection and no more than five days of symptoms. At three months, require a lower proportion reporting at least one of fatigue, breathlessness or cognitive symptoms (memory or concentration problems) in the intention-to-treat comparison, at two-sided p<0.05.
milestones.set_by: PANORAMIC Norway investigators, NCT05852873, protocol sections 5.3.1 and 5.7.
milestones.threshold_quote: The standard cut-off of p<0.05 will be used for statistical significance levels.

milestones.title: A randomized prevention trial shows greater clinical benefit in the prespecified marker-positive group.
milestones.criterion: Measure the candidate marker before treatment. Compare early treatment with control in both marker-positive and marker-negative adults on the same prespecified clinical long COVID endpoint. Test the difference between the two treatment effects on the prespecified scale and demonstrate greater preventive benefit in the marker-positive group.
milestones.set_by: FDA–NIH Biomarker Working Group, BEST framework for distinguishing predictive from prognostic biomarkers, applied to a randomized prevention trial.
milestones.threshold_quote: a comparison of a treatment to a control in patients with and without the biomarker.

not_found: No independent randomized trials were found linking pretreatment marker status and pathway engagement to prevention of function-limiting long COVID.
No guideline or research programme was found that judged biomarker-guided prevention of long COVID unachievable or unworthy of study.

results.finding: In COVID-OUT (n=1,126), metformin reduced clinician-diagnosed long COVID through day 300 versus matched placebo (two-sided log-rank p=0.012).
results.quote: The cumulative incidence of long COVID by day 300 was 6·3% (95% CI 4·2–8·2) in participants who received metformin and 10·4% (7·8–12·9) in those who received identical metformin placebo (hazard ratio [HR] 0·59, 95% CI 0·39–0·89; p=0·012).

results.finding: Metformin’s infectious SARS-CoV-2 IC50 in Calu3 cells was 0.4 mM (n=3 biological replicates per condition).
results.detail: The separate viability assay covered both mock-infected and infected cultures.
results.quote: IC50 values from dose-variation studies in infected cells were found to be 0.4 and 1.43 mM in Calu3 and Caco2 cells, respectively.

results.finding: Pomotrelvir against infectious SARS-CoV-2 WA-1 in iPS-AT2 cells had a mean plaque-assay EC50 of 32 nM (4–12 experiments across assays).
results.detail: Table 2 provides the experiment-count range across assays and leaves the exact plaque-assay count unspecified. DMSO normalization is explicitly described for the separate reporter-based combination assay.
results.quote: The mean EC50 values of 32 nM (by plaque assay) and 36 nM (by qRT-PCR) in the SARS CoV-2 assay in iPS-AT2 cells

results.finding: PANORAMIC Norway (n=144) found a lower three-month symptom proportion with nirmatrelvir–ritonavir than with placebo (p=0.039).
results.detail: Recruitment stopped early at 144 of a planned 2,000 participants. The excerpt describes the cognitive component in general terms.
results.quote: corresponding to a relative risk after imputation of data for the single missing value in the placebo group of 0·60 (95% CI 0·37–0·98; p=0·039).
